language_wrapper: Find the least positive integer n such that, no matter how {base}^n is expressed as the product of {k} positive integers, at least one of these integers has a digit zero somewhere in its base-{base} representation.
hardness_rationale: The seed asks for k=2 and exploits a simple observation: to avoid a digit zero, neither factor can be divisible by 10, forcing consideration of 2^n and 5^n only. Our family expands to an arbitrary k, turning the problem into a constrained decomposition problem: you must simultaneously express n as sums of exponents drawn from those for which 2^a and 5^b are zero-free in base 10. The necessity to optimize the number of terms in two separate unbounded coin-change problems (for 2 and 5) and to reason about their combined bound f_A(n) + f_B(n) > k increases the difficulty substantially. It requires deeper structural insight and dynamic programming rather than simple casework or guessing.
notes: Proof sketch of correctness: Let 10^n = 2^n 5^n be factored into k positive integers. If any factor includes both prime 2 and prime 5 to a positive power, it is divisible by 10 and thus has a trailing digit zero, violating zero-freeness. Therefore, in any zero-free factorization, each nontrivial factor must be a pure power of 2 or of 5, and the product of all 2-powers must be 2^n while that of all 5-powers must be 5^n. Let A = {a >= 1 : 2^a has no zero in base-10} and B = {b >= 1 : 5^b has no zero in base-10}. Define f_A(n) to be the minimal number of elements of A (with repetition allowed) whose sum is n (similarly f_B(n)). Then a zero-free k-factorization exists if and only if f_A(n) + f_B(n) <= k, because we can use f_A(n) many zero-free powers of 2 and f_B(n) many zero-free powers of 5, padding with 1's to reach exactly k factors. Consequently, the least n such that every k-factorization forces at least one zero digit is exactly the least n for which f_A(n) + f_B(n) > k. The verifier implements this logic via dynamic programming to compute f_A(n) and f_B(n) and searches for the minimal n. This retains the core idea from the seed (digit-zero constraints on 10-smooth numbers) but generalizes to an optimization over multiple factors. Implementation note: We restrict base to 10 to preserve the trailing-zero characterization and avoid subtleties with other bases where divisibility thresholds for trailing zeros differ (e.g., b = 2^a 5^c with a, c > 1).
source_question: Find the least positive integer $n$ such that no matter how $10^{n}$ is expressed as the product of any two positive integers, at least one of these two integers contains the digit $0$ .
